analysis.one_liner: Bans all US greenhouse gas rules until China, India, and Russia adopt similar cuts.
analysis.headline: Introduced with zero cosponsors and referred to committee, the bill never received a hearing or vote and died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would forbid any federal agency from issuing or enforcing any rule that cuts carbon dioxide or other greenhouse gas emissions — including rules already on the books — until the EPA, the Energy Information Administration, and the Commerce Department certify in writing that China, India, and Russia have adopted and are enforcing substantially similar reductions. Any such rule in effect before that certification would be nullified. It was introduced by one senator, attracted no cosponsors, and never came up in committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal, oil, and gas producers and coal-fired power plants would gain the most: the bill would wipe out EPA carbon rules, including the Clean Power Plan then underway, and would bar any future greenhouse gas regulation until foreign governments acted. Energy-intensive industries facing compliance costs would also benefit. Consumers might see marginally lower energy prices in the near term, at the cost of unaddressed climate and air-quality risks.

how_it_helps.text: It would immediately strip all existing federal greenhouse gas regulations of force, not just block new ones [S3].

It would give China, India, and Russia effective veto power over US climate rules, since no regulation could take effect until those three countries adopted and enforced substantially similar reductions [S3].
It would apply to every federal agency, not just the EPA, so no department could act on emissions reductions of any kind [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the costs of unchecked carbon pollution: more severe climate impacts (stronger storms, heat waves, sea-level rise) and continued air pollution that falls hardest on communities near power plants and industrial facilities. Future taxpayers would also carry the cost of adapting to climate change that earlier rules could have limited.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities facing pollution and climate harm

drawbacks.text: The bill would nullify regulations already in effect, abruptly unraveling programs that utilities and states had begun implementing and creating regulatory uncertainty [S3].

The certification standard is vague — 'substantially similar' reductions by three foreign governments, judged by US agencies — making compliance effectively open-ended and the freeze potentially permanent [S3].
By tying all US action to three specific countries, it would prevent the United States from meeting any international climate commitment or acting even where cost-effective reductions are available.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is short-term regulatory relief for fossil energy producers and some avoided compliance costs. Its cost is a complete, potentially indefinite halt to US greenhouse gas regulation — including rules already in force — with the resulting climate and public-health burdens falling on the public. The measure was a statement bill: it had no cosponsors and no path to passage, so its practical effect was nil.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and sent to the Environment and Public Works Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. David Vitter introduced the bill on January 7, 2015, the opening week of the 114th Congress [S1].
It had no cosponsors at any point [S4].
Its only action was being read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on the day of introduction [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever occurred, and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people kept the regulatory status quo: EPA greenhouse gas rules, including the Clean Power Plan, were not nullified and could proceed through the normal legal process. Coal, oil, and gas producers did not get the sweeping deregulation the bill promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public kept EPA climate rules intact

for.name: Sen. David Vitter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Environment and Public Works Committee.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: One Republican senator sponsored the bill and not a single member of either party cosponsored it, so no meaningful coalition formed on either side.

industries.note: The bill would have nullified EPA carbon rules and barred new ones indefinitely, removing compliance costs and keeping fossil fuels unregulated for emissions. The cost of that deregulation — climate damage and local air pollution — would fall on the public rather than the industry.

By voiding the Clean Power Plan and similar rules, the bill would spare coal-heavy utilities the expense of shifting generation. It would also delay cleaner air in the communities surrounding their plants.

A freeze on all federal greenhouse gas rules would remove the regulatory pressure driving demand for wind, solar, and pollution-control equipment, slowing investment that many communities and workers had counted on.
